claim: A deterministic AST-analysis post-processing framework that validates generated code against a dynamically-generated, library-introspection-built Knowledge Base can detect Knowledge Conflicting Hallucinations (e.g. non-existent API parameters/function names) with 100% precision and 87.6% recall (F1 = 0.934) on a manually curated 200-snippet Python dataset.
stance_target: deterministic static-analysis verification is a viable, reliable alternative to probabilistic LLM-in-the-loop hallucination repair
quoted_support: On a manually-curated dataset of 200 Python snippets, our framework detected KCHs with 100% precision and 87.6% recall (0.934 F1-score), and successfully auto-corrected 77.0% of all identified hallucinations.

claim: Knowledge Conflicting Hallucinations in LLM-generated code (e.g. calling a non-existent pandas function pd.read_exel()) are syntactically clean and idiomatic-looking but fail only at runtime, meaning linters and standard static checks cannot catch them.
stance_target: structural/syntactic analysis alone is insufficient to catch a specific, common class of LLM code hallucination
scope_conditions: LLM code generation, Python ecosystem example
quoted_support: a model may call pd.read_exel('data.csv'), which both invents a function name and mismatches the intended file type... This failure often presents as a block of code that looks clean, seems idiomatic, and even follows local variable naming conventions. But when executed, the program crashes.
